grammarNotes.title: war and hatte: was and had
grammarNotes.body:
**sein** and **haben** have their own short past forms, and Germans use them all the time:

- *Ich **war** krank.* = I was ill.
- *Ich **hatte** keine Zeit.* = I didn't have time.

Like the modal verbs, **ich** and **er / sie / es** look the same and have no ending.

To ask about something that's over, use **Wie war …?**: *Wie war das Wochenende?*

grammarNotes.title: The Perfekt: talking about the past
grammarNotes.body:
Spoken German uses the **Perfekt** for most things that happened in the past. It has two parts:

- a form of **haben** (or *sein*) in second place
- the **past participle** at the very end

It works like a modal verb: the second part waits at the end. One Perfekt covers English *I played*, *I have played* and *I did play*.

You can start with a time. *haben* stays second, so *ich* moves after it.

grammarNotes.title: Making the past participle
grammarNotes.body:
Most participles start with **ge-**:

- **Regular verbs**: ge- + stem + **-t**. If the stem ends in *-t*, add an *e*: *gearbeitet*.
- **Irregular verbs**: ge- + stem + **-en**, and the vowel sometimes changes. Learn these by heart.
- **Separable verbs**: **ge** goes between the prefix and the verb, all in one word: *eingekauft*.
- **No ge-** for verbs ending in **-ieren** and verbs starting with **be-**: *telefoniert, besucht*.

grammarNotes.title: haben or sein?
grammarNotes.body:
Most verbs use **haben**. A small group uses **sein**: verbs of **moving from one place to another**, plus **bleiben** (to stay). For now, learn these five: *gehen, fahren, kommen, aufstehen, bleiben*. You also know *passieren* from **Was ist passiert?**

For *sein* and *haben* themselves, use **war** and **hatte** instead of the Perfekt: *Ich war krank. Ich hatte Fieber.*

Don't mix up **nach Hause** (going home) and **zu Hause** (at home).
table: Er ist um acht Uhr gekommen.
Ich bin um sieben Uhr aufgestanden.

grammarNotes.title: Time words for the past
grammarNotes.body:
Like *heute* and *morgen*, these need no *am* or *im*. Put one first and the verb still comes second: *Gestern **war** ich müde.*

**letzte Woche** and **letztes Jahr** are fixed phrases: the ending of *letzt-* matches the noun (*die Woche, das Jahr*).

**schon** (already) and **noch nicht** (not yet) go in the middle, before the participle: *Ich habe **noch nicht** gegessen.*

exercises.title: gestern: yesterday
exercises.body:
Time to talk about the past! Start with two time words:

- **gestern** = yesterday
- **vorgestern** = the day before yesterday

You know *heute, morgen* and *übermorgen*. Now you can go the other way. Like *heute*, they need no *am*.

exercises.title: war: was
exercises.body:
**sein** (to be) has a short past form: **war** = was.

- ich **war** = I was
- du **warst** = you were
- er / sie / es **war** = he / she / it was
- wir **waren** = we were
- ihr **wart** = you (all) were
- sie / Sie **waren** = they were / you were (formal)

Just like the modal verbs, *ich* and *er / sie* look the same and have no ending.

examples.text: Wir waren am Wochenende in Berlin.
examples.translation: We were in Berlin at the weekend.

accepted: war

exercises.instruction: Which form fits? Wir ___ am Wochenende in Wien.
exercises.prompt: We were in Vienna at the weekend.

exercises.title: hatte: had
exercises.body:
**haben** has a past form too: **hatte** = had.

- ich **hatte**
- du **hattest**
- er / sie / es **hatte**
- wir **hatten**
- ihr **hattet**
- sie / Sie **hatten**

A sentence you'll use a lot: **Ich hatte keine Zeit.** = I didn't have time.

accepted: hatte

exercises.title: Wie war …? How was …?
exercises.body:
To ask about something that's over, say **Wie war …?** = How was …?

Answer with *war* too:

- **toll** = great
- **gut** = good
- **langweilig** = boring

**die Party** is the English word, said the German way: *PAR-tee*.

exercises.instruction: A friend asks you this. The film was boring. What do you say?

accepted: Ich war gestern müde.
Gestern war ich müde.

lessons.title: What did you do? The Perfekt

exercises.title: The Perfekt
exercises.body:
For most verbs, spoken German talks about the past with the **Perfekt**. It has two parts:

- a form of **haben** in second place
- the **past participle** at the very end

*Ich **habe** Fußball **gespielt**.* = I played football.

It works just like a modal verb, where the second verb waits at the end. And one Perfekt covers *I played*, *I have played* and *I did play*.

exercises.title: ge- … -t
exercises.body:
For regular verbs, the participle is easy. Take the stem (the verb without *-en*), put **ge-** in front and **-t** at the end:

- spiel*en* → **ge**spiel**t**
- mach*en* → **ge**mach**t**
- kauf*en* → **ge**kauf**t**

If the stem ends in *-t*, add an extra *e*, just like in *er arbeitet*: arbeit*en* → **ge**arbeit**et**.

accepted: gespielt

exercises.title: Was hast du gemacht?
exercises.body:
To ask *What did you do?*, put **machen** in the Perfekt: **Was hast du gemacht?** To someone you call *Sie*: **Was haben Sie gemacht?**

You can start with a time. *haben* stays second, so *ich* moves after it: ***Gestern** habe ich gearbeitet.*

Two fixed phrases for further back: **letzte Woche** = last week, **letztes Jahr** = last year. Like *gestern*, they need no *am* or *im*.

examples.text: Letzte Woche habe ich eine Jacke gekauft.
examples.translation: Last week I bought a jacket.

examples.text: Letztes Jahr habe ich in Wien gewohnt.
examples.translation: Last year I lived in Vienna.

exercises.translation: Last week I learned German. (start with last week)
exercises.answer: Letzte Woche habe ich Deutsch gelernt.

exercises.title: besuchen and telefonieren: no ge-
exercises.body:
Two kinds of verbs don't take **ge-**:

- verbs ending in **-ieren**: *telefonieren* (to talk on the phone) → **telefoniert**
- verbs starting with **be-**: *besuchen* (to visit) → **besucht**

They still end in *-t* and still use *haben*. Don't mix up *telefonieren* (having a phone conversation) with *anrufen* (calling someone).

Did you talk to Anna on the phone?

exercises.title: ge- … -en
exercises.body:
Many everyday verbs are **irregular**: their participle ends in **-en** instead of *-t*. They still use *haben*:

- essen → **gegessen**
- trinken → **getrunken**
- lesen → **gelesen**
- sehen → **gesehen**
- schlafen → **geschlafen**

There's no rule to tell you which verbs do this, so learn each participle with its verb.

accepted: getrunken
exercises.translation: I drank two cups of coffee.
exercises.hint: trinken → participle (-en, and the vowel changes)

exercises.title: Vowel changes
exercises.body:
Some participles change their vowel too:

- trinken → getr**u**nken
- treffen → getr**o**ffen
- sprechen → gespr**o**chen
- schreiben → geschr**ie**ben

**schreiben** = to write, and **die Nachricht** = the message. A text on your phone is a *Nachricht* too.

exercises.title: Separable verbs: ge in the middle
exercises.body:
With separable verbs, **ge** goes *between* the prefix and the verb, all in one word:

- einkaufen → ein**ge**kauft
- fernsehen → fern**ge**sehen
- anrufen → an**ge**rufen

The stress stays on the prefix: **EIN**gekauft, **FERN**gesehen, **AN**gerufen.

accepted: eingekauft

exercises.title: schon and noch nicht
exercises.body:
- **schon** = already
- **noch nicht** = not yet

They go in the middle, before the participle: *Ich habe **schon** gegessen.*

In a question, *schon* is often just English *yet*: *Hast du **schon** gegessen?* = Have you eaten yet?

lessons.title: I went: the Perfekt with sein

exercises.title: Some verbs use sein
exercises.body:
A few verbs make the Perfekt with **sein** instead of *haben*. Mostly they're verbs of **moving from one place to another**:

- gehen → ich **bin** … **gegangen**
- fahren → ich **bin** … **gefahren**
- kommen → ich **bin** … **gekommen**

You know **nach** from Unit 12: *nach Berlin* = to Berlin, *nach Hause* = home.

examples.text: Er ist um zehn Uhr gekommen.
Bist du mit dem Bus gefahren?

accepted: sind

exercises.title: aufstehen and bleiben
exercises.body:
Two more *sein* verbs you'll use every day:

- **aufstehen** → ich **bin** um sieben Uhr **aufgestanden**. Getting out of bed is a move too!
- **bleiben** (to stay) → ich **bin** zu Hause **geblieben**. *bleiben* is the odd one out: no movement, but still *sein*.

Remember **zu Hause** (at home) from Unit 13.

examples.text: Ich bin um sieben Uhr aufgestanden.
examples.translation: I got up at seven o'clock.

exercises.instruction: haben or sein? Ich ___ gestern zu Hause geblieben.
haben or sein? Wir ___ einen Film gesehen.

exercises.title: Was ist passiert?
exercises.body:
**Was ist passiert?** = What happened? *passieren* uses **sein**, and it has no *ge-* because it ends in *-ieren*.

To answer with *sein* or *haben* themselves, don't use the Perfekt: use **war** and **hatte**.

examples.text: Ich hatte Fieber und bin zu Hause geblieben.
examples.translation: I had a temperature and stayed at home.

exercises.title: Urlaub, Reise, Foto
exercises.body:
- **der Urlaub** = holiday, time off work. **im Urlaub** = on holiday.
- **die Reise** = the journey, the trip
- **das Foto** = the photo. In German you *make* photos: **Fotos machen** = to take photos.

examples.text: Wir sind im Urlaub nach Italien gefahren.
examples.translation: We went to Italy on holiday.

exercises.title: Talking about the weekend
exercises.body:
Three more words for Monday morning:

- **lange** = for a long time. **lange schlafen** = to sleep in.
- **der Ausflug** = the day trip, the outing. **einen Ausflug machen** = to go on a day trip.
- **Schade!** = What a pity! Shame!

examples.translation: We went on a day trip.

exercises.title: A1 checkpoint
exercises.body:
You've reached the end of A1! This lesson mixes everything from Units 1 to 14:

- greetings and numbers
- *einen* and *kein* after *möchten* and *es gibt*
- telling the time
- verb second, *gern* and modal verbs
- *den*, colours and prices
- *mit dem* and *zum*
- *wehtun*
- *war, hatte* and the Perfekt

Got something wrong? No problem: look back at that unit's grammar notes.
